answer.rationale: Three constraints bind at once: an 18% cost mandate, a hard 14-day expiry with no auto-renew, and 94% line loading with zero buffer. The zero-buffer condition is decisive against switch_primary_vendor this cycle: memory_c2's low-cost-vendor win is the most attractive on cost, but it was recorded 'last year' under unstated volume and buffer conditions, and a migration inside 14 days at 94% utilization converts a cost problem into a delivery-failure problem, which the primary objective explicitly forbids. defer_decision borrows from memory_c5, but that record is explicitly about a NON-CRITICAL service that continued month-to-month; this contract is critical and does not auto-renew, so the analogy does not transfer. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but does not deliver 18% and cannot stand up a qualified alternate inside 14 days. That leaves the incumbent path. The incumbent has refused to reopen price THIS CYCLE, which forecloses the memory_c4 lever as stated but not the memory_c6 lever: term length and volume commitment are a different currency than in-cycle price. So memory_c6 is the load-bearing memory and the one I spend my single verification on. I need the source record to answer what the consolidated line hides: was it this component category and this supplier, what term length and volume floor were actually committed, and did the lock later cost flexibility or absorb a demand drop? If c6 turns out to be a different category or a supplier with different leverage, the multi-year lever is weaker than the summary implies and I fall back to a short bridge at benchmarked rates. I am deliberately scoping this as a guarded test rather than the full multi-year lock the memory invites: a short bridge extension that secures continuity past the expiry, prices against external benchmarks (memory_c4's mechanism, which is about benchmarking pressure and survives the price refusal), and buys an option on volume pricing without committing years of exposure. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: a long incumbent lock would foreclose the memory_c2 low-cost path and the memory_c3 dual-source path precisely when the cost mandate makes both valuable, and it concentrates single-point-of-failure risk that memory_c3 says is worth removing. I also note the 18% target is probably not reachable from this one decision; I would rather capture partial savings and preserve the option to qualify a second source next cycle than book a full multi-year commitment to hit a number this cycle. Residual uncertainty stays open: none of these memories record what happened under a zero-buffer line, which is the condition that actually governs here.
